stories.body: President Donald Trump said the war with Iran would end “very soon,” without giving details, while reiterating that Tehran would not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon. The claim came amid reports of shipping incidents in the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global oil and gas supplies.
stories.headline: Trump says Iran war will end soon as shipping incidents are reported in the Strait of Hormuz

stories.body: US forces completed their withdrawal from Iraq under an agreement reached during Joe Biden's presidency, ending the advisory deployment that remained from the anti-ISIS coalition. Iraq marked the exit with a new Sovereignty Days holiday, but officials and analysts warned that the departure could give Iran-backed militias greater influence and create space for ISIS to rebuild. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi is seeking to strengthen state control over weapons and disarm militias by 2027, but some powerful pro-Iran groups have indicated they will resist.
stories.headline: United States completes withdrawal of its remaining troops from Iraq, raising fears of a security vacuum

stories.body: At least five people, including a 14-year-old child, were killed and several others wounded in a new Russian overnight attack on Kyiv and nearby areas. The strikes also briefly prompted the closure of airports in Lublin and Rzeszow, Poland. Ukraine's economy minister said air-raid alerts cost the country an estimated $45 million for every hour that businesses shut down, as attacks on industrial sites, warehouses, logistics hubs and data centres intensify; the government has introduced a two-tier warning system intended to let some businesses remain open during drone alerts.
stories.headline: Russian strikes on Kyiv kill several people as Ukraine counts the economic cost of missile alerts

stories.body: Trump and the leaders of Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, xAI and Nvidia signed a voluntary agreement pledging stronger safeguards for frontier AI systems. The accord calls for internal controls, monitoring teams, board oversight and independent audits, though it does not specify who would conduct third-party evaluations. Trump presented self-regulation as preferable to new government restrictions, despite international calls for formal AI rules and warnings from some industry leaders about catastrophic risks.
stories.headline: Trump and major technology companies sign voluntary AI-safety accord, relying on industry self-regulation

stories.body: King Mohammed VI appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri, Marrakesh's mayor and urban planning minister, as Morocco's first woman prime minister. Her monarchy-aligned Authenticity and Modernity Party won 97 of 395 parliamentary seats, leaving her to assemble a coalition. El Mansouri called the appointment historic and becomes the third woman to serve as prime minister in the Arab world; her incoming government will also oversee major investment decisions ahead of Morocco's co-hosting of the 2030 World Cup.
stories.headline: Morocco appoints Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as the country's first woman prime minister

stories.body: South Korea demanded an apology and corrective action from North Korea after two explosions during a September 21 search operation injured three South Korean soldiers just south of the military demarcation line. A joint investigation by the UN Command and South Korea's military found a live North Korean anti-personnel mine on the southern side of the border and concluded that an armistice violation had occurred. Pyongyang denied responsibility, with Kim Jong-un's sister Kim Yo-jong calling the incident staged and threatening retaliation if South Korean forces fired at North Korean troops.
stories.headline: South Korea demands an apology from North Korea after landmine explosions injure three soldiers near the DMZ

stories.body: The Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to resume deporting migrants to countries other than their own while it considers the legality of the policy. The court's conservative majority temporarily lifted safeguards that had required deportees to be told where they would be sent and given time to raise fears of persecution, with a final ruling still to come after further arguments.
stories.headline: Supreme Court allows the Trump administration to resume third-country deportations for now

stories.body: Entrepreneur Ken Griffin donated $3 billion to Carnegie Mellon University, the largest gift ever made to a university. The donation will support the institution's Pittsburgh campus and establish a new campus in Miami.
stories.headline: Carnegie Mellon receives a $3 billion gift, the largest donation ever made to a university

stories.body: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has moved to prevent US military academies from hiring civilian faculty members into tenured professorships. The step is the latest effort by the Trump administration to exert greater control over faculty at service academies.
stories.headline: Hegseth moves to bar military academies from hiring civilian faculty as tenured professors

stories.body: Spain's government approved two housing decrees that will face a parliamentary vote on Friday, including an extension of eviction protections for vulnerable tenants in certain properties until the end of 2030 and up to two years of annual extensions for eligible leases ending before 2029. The package also proposes rules for seasonal and room rentals, restrictions on purchases by certain investment funds, tax changes for real-estate investment companies and a reduced 10% VAT rate for tourist rentals. The government has not yet secured the support needed from Junts, the PNV and Podemos.
stories.headline: Spain's government unveils housing decrees extending eviction protections and seeking greater stability for tenants

stories.body: Spain's Defence Ministry sent Amnesty International's allegations of abuse by military personnel against migrants in Ceuta to prosecutors and the city's duty court, and ordered the Operations Command to investigate possible individual responsibility. Amnesty says it documented assaults and degrading treatment that may amount to torture, as well as inadequate reception conditions, after interviewing more than 65 migrants and asylum seekers, including minors and pregnant women, during a visit this month. The inquiry comes two months after a mass arrival from Morocco overwhelmed the city.
stories.headline: Spain refers Amnesty International's allegations of military abuse of migrants in Ceuta to prosecutors and a court

stories.body: Two months after the mass arrival of migrants into Ceuta, the crisis has shifted from an acute security emergency toward a continuing humanitarian emergency. Authorities say 7,794 people have returned voluntarily to Morocco and 449 have been expelled, with police attributing the rising rate of voluntary departures to physical and psychological exhaustion as well as declining financial and logistical support. Migrants remaining in the city continue to face precarious conditions, while police have moved groups from beach encampments to the Loma Colmenar site.
stories.headline: Ceuta continues to grapple with the migrant crisis two months after the mass border crossing, as returns increase

stories.body: King Felipe VI called on France to speed up long-delayed electricity, rail and hydrogen connections with Spain during a Spanish-French business forum attended by President Emmanuel Macron. The king described the projects as essential for competitiveness, energy security and European integration. Cross-border electricity capacity remains limited to 2.5 GW, although a Bay of Biscay subsea link under construction is expected to raise it to 5 GW in 2028; France previously opposed the MidCat gas pipeline, which was replaced by the planned H2Med hydrogen corridor.
stories.headline: King Felipe VI urges France to accelerate energy and rail interconnections during Macron's state visit

stories.body: Catalan housing groups said the Spanish government's new housing decrees do not match the scale of the housing crisis and vowed to keep protesting. The Socialist Housing Union of Catalonia called the measures inadequate and demanded deeper intervention, including halving rents and expropriating homes owned by investment funds, while other tenant groups welcomed parts of the package but warned they would scrutinize loopholes. A protest has been called for Saturday in L'Hospitalet de Llobregat, with a march planned from Barcelona's Plaça d'Espanya.
stories.headline: Barcelona housing activists say Spain's new housing measures fall short and plan further protests

stories.body: September 2026 was the hottest September recorded at Barcelona's Fabra Observatory in more than a century of observations, with a provisional average temperature of 24.8C, 1.3C above the previous record and nearly 4C above the reference average. Twenty-seven of the month's 30 days were warmer than normal. The month was also wetter than usual, with 155 litres per square metre of rain compared with a normal 80, although 83% of the total fell in just two episodes, including torrential storms on September 29.
stories.headline: September becomes Barcelona's hottest on record at the Fabra Observatory, with nearly double the normal rainfall

stories.body: Torrential rain damaged roads and cut access through several of Barcelona's hill neighborhoods, with landslides, rocks and vegetation blocking streets in Sant Genís dels Agudells, Torre Baró and Can Rectoret. A landslide on Carrer de Cànoves forced a road closure and diverted a local bus route, while residents in Torre Baró organized their own cleanup after debris stopped bus service. Elsewhere in the metropolitan area, firefighters rescued a woman and her five-month-old baby after their car became trapped in rising water in Gavà; emergency services received more than 1,400 weather-related calls by early afternoon.
stories.headline: Heavy rain leaves mountain-neighborhood roads impassable and cuts off parts of Barcelona

stories.body: About 250 workers at the Port of Barcelona protested against a proposal to use future public-sector wage increases to correct what the port calls an accumulated technical payroll discrepancy. The issue stems from a state audit that found a difference between the authorized wage bill and payments made under certain compensation categories. Workers, who also protested in July, argue that there are other ways to resolve the problem and urge the port not to accept the audit's conclusion without further review.
stories.headline: Barcelona port workers protest proposed salary reductions linked to an accumulated payroll discrepancy
